record.title: Preprint reports AI-assisted reproduction and robustness screening across 20 SEER studies
record.summary: The authors introduce SEER-Repro, a curated benchmark of 20 published studies using the U.S. Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) cancer registry, and report that an AI coding agent reproduced 1,694 of 2,190 atomic claims (77.4%). A separate agentic analysis pipeline flagged 55 of 579 reproduced findings (9.5%) for expert review. One coauthor manually examined 10 flagged cases: nine did not establish a consequential change under a defensible alternative, while one needs further statistical review. These are paper-reported results from one curated biomedical data corpus, not independent proof of general clinical audit capability.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that their AI coding agent reproduced 1,694 of 2,190 atomic claims (77.4%) across 20 selected SEER-based papers; 76 were close and 420 were not reproduced.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that their agentic robustness pipeline flagged 55 of 579 fully reproduced findings (9.5%) for expert review; one coauthor reviewed 10 cases, with nine not establishing a consequential change under a defensible alternative and one requiring further review.

claims.label: INFERRED
claims.text: Claim-level reproduction and alternative-analysis screening may help direct scarce expert attention toward research findings that merit closer review, if the reported process transfers beyond this curated corpus.

evidence_gaps.description: The reported 77.4% rate and robustness-screening outcomes have not been independently reproduced; this review did not establish public access to the exact benchmark/code package.
Only 10 model-flagged cases received coauthor review in this paper, and the corpus covers 20 SEER studies; clinical validity and transfer beyond this setting remain unknown.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported workflow can reproduce prior findings and prioritize robustness checks reliably, it could expand scientific audit capacity in evidence-heavy biomedical research. The demonstrated scope is one curated SEER corpus of 20 papers, with substantial manual data curation and expert review of only 10 flagged cases.
limitations: The results are author-reported in a preprint and have not been independently reproduced in this review.
The benchmark covers 20 selected SEER studies, not a representative sample of all medical or scientific literature.
The authors classify 420 non-reproduced claims; data issues are the largest category and 48 cases (11.4%) are attributed to agent-side errors.
The robustness system's 55 flagged cases are model-assessed leads, not established errors in the original papers; a coauthor reviewed only 10 and one remained unresolved.
No exact public implementation or benchmark release was located or tested in this review.

The prior-art comparison inspected primary abstracts/metadata for CORE-Bench, REPRO-Bench and RECLAIM, not their full protocols or artifacts; it narrows the novelty claim but is not an exhaustive literature review.
brief.summary: The authors introduce SEER-Repro, a curated benchmark of 20 published studies using the U.S. Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) cancer registry, and report that an AI coding agent reproduced 1,694 of 2,190 atomic claims (77.4%). A separate agentic analysis pipeline flagged 55 of 579 reproduced findings (9.5%) for expert review. One coauthor manually examined 10 flagged cases: nine did not establish a consequential change under a defensible alternative, while one needs further statistical review. These are paper-reported results from one curated biomedical data corpus, not independent proof of general clinical audit capability.

technical.claimed_result: The preprint reports 77.4% reproduction across 2,190 atomic claims and a model-generated robustness-review shortlist covering 55/579 fully reproduced findings.
technical.demonstrated_result: No independent result is established by this review; the reported rates and evaluations are claims made in the preprint.
technical.mechanism: A coding agent reconstructs published SEER findings from papers, registry data and documentation; a second pipeline proposes defensible analytical alternatives, reruns analyses where feasible and prioritizes potentially consequential changes for expert review.
technical.novelty: The contribution is domain-specific: the authors apply claim-level reproduction and alternative-analysis screening to a curated SEER medical-epidemiology corpus. Prior agent benchmarks already assess paper reproduction or reproducibility judgments across wider scientific and social-science collections, so this should not be described as the first general paper-reproduction benchmark.
technical.regime: 20 selected SEER-based papers (10 highly cited and 10 more recent), 2,190 atomic claims, 39 data tables and 40 documentation resources; authors report using GPT-5.6 Sol xhigh for reproduction and multiple models for robustness analysis.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint describes packaged data, documentation, executable baselines and evidence traces, but this review did not retrieve or independently run a public implementation or benchmark package.
technical.strongest_baseline: Prior adjacent benchmarks include CORE-Bench (90 papers/270 tasks across computer science, social science and medicine), REPRO-Bench (112 social-science reproducibility-assessment tasks), and RECLAIM (100 NeurIPS 2025 papers with fixed claims and GPU-hour budgets). These are not matched baselines for the reported SEER reproduction rate; this review compared primary abstracts/metadata, not artifacts or full protocols.

brief.title: Preprint reports AI-assisted reproduction and robustness screening across 20 SEER studies
brief.why_it_matters: Claim-level reproduction and explicit testing of alternative analytic choices could make some scientific review cheaper and more systematic. The paper’s own results show why expert review remains necessary: its 55 model-flagged findings were leads, and only one of ten examined cases remained potentially consequential.
